name: Kambo frog venom ritual

card.summary: A ritual in which secretion from the giant leaf frog is applied to small skin burns, which practitioners describe as a purge that leaves the body feeling cleansed and energised.
card.note: Documented hospitalisations and deaths; banned or restricted in several countries.

quick.overview:
Kambo is a traditional Amazonian practice in which dried skin secretion of the giant leaf frog (Phyllomedusa bicolor) is applied to small, deliberate burns on the skin. Participants typically experience a rapid purge with nausea and vomiting, and many describe it afterwards as a cleanse.
In wellness circles the practice is linked to ideas of detox, clearer skin, energy and mental clarity, which is how it reaches appearance-focused communities. Published reviews have documented its acute effects and adverse events; they have not established the claimed health benefits.
quick.how: In Indigenous settings the secretion is collected from a restrained frog, dried, and applied to small burns on the skin. Outside South America, practitioners run one-on-one or group sessions, applying reconstituted secretion to burns on the upper arm or leg, often with water drinking beforehand and a purge afterwards.
quick.risks: Common effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, fast heartbeat, low blood pressure and facial swelling. Excess water intake has been linked to dangerous electrolyte imbalance, and reviews describe severe cases including organ injury, oesophageal rupture and seizures, plus a small number of deaths. Brazil banned its sale and marketing in 2004 and Australia's TGA scheduled it as a poison in 2021.

lead: Kambo (also called sapo or vacina-do-sapo) is a substance obtained from the skin secretion of the giant leaf frog, Phyllomedusa bicolor, of the Amazon and Orinoco basins. It began as folk medicine and ritual among Panoan-speaking peoples such as the Matsés and Katukina [1].

Within wellness and fringe self-improvement communities it is discussed as a detox or cleansing ritual. Promoters say it brings energy, mental clarity and a sense of renewal, and some describe the resulting vitality and complexion as part of looking healthier; this is the practitioner framing, and the appearance link is indirect [1].
Reviews of case reports describe acute intoxications and some deaths, and the Wikipedia summary notes that the health claims are not supported by scientific studies [1].

angle.text: Practitioners present kambo as a purge that leaves them feeling cleansed and energised, which some tie to looking fresher and healthier. This is a claimed, indirect link; the documented effects are an acute physiological reaction.

paras: In traditional use the frog is restrained so that it releases skin secretion, and is then released unharmed. The secretion is dried and later applied to small burns made on the skin [1].
Outside South America, practitioners make superficial burns on the upper arm or leg with a smoldering stick and apply the reconstituted secretion, in individual sessions or group kambo circles [1].

Among Panoan peoples such as the Matsés and Katukina it is a ritual with spiritual meaning. Since the mid-20th century it has been practised in Brazilian cities, and it became known as an alternative therapy outside South America in the late 2010s [1].
Promoters claim it helps with addiction, depression, chronic pain, fevers, fertility, energy and mental clarity, and that it removes negative energy [1].

No controlled clinical trials of kambo's claimed benefits are known. Research consists mainly of case reports and reviews: a 2022 review identified 11 acute intoxication cases with severe outcomes including psychosis, kidney and liver injury, oesophageal rupture and seizures, and a 2025 systematic review found few fatal cases and noted that pre-existing conditions may worsen outcomes [1]. Naloxone has been studied as a possible antidote [1].
Common effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, tachycardia, low blood pressure and facial swelling. Drinking excess water has been linked to SIADH and severe electrolyte imbalance [1].

Deaths reported in the literature and press include cases in Brazil (2008), Chile (2009), Italy (2018), the 2019 death of Natasha Lechner, an Australian festival death in 2021 involving kambo and DMT, and a UK death in 2026 [1].

Brazil banned sale and marketing in 2004, importing it is illegal in Chile, and in 2021 Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration made it a Schedule 10 poison. The Australian Medical Association supported the ban, calling it a significant health risk [1].
